questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select No improvement. Under each category their is so much scope for minor variations so there is immense ingenuity in costume designing now than ever before.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select No improvement.

Under each category their is so much scope for minor variations so there is immense ingenuity in costume designing now than ever before.
questions.solution: The highlighted phrase contains 'their' (which means belonging to or associated with the people or things previously mentioned) which needs to be replaced by 'there'. In option b) use of 'more' is incorrect as it is used to make comparison in a sentence. In option c) use of 'many' for 'scopes' is incorrect in the given sentence as 'scope' (here means the opportunity or possibility to do or deal with something) is not a countable noun. Hence, the answer is option a).

questions.solution:
The phrase 'not only' is accompanied with either 'but' or 'but also' in the sentence. Only option (c) can suffice this condition.

questions.solution: As the correct preposition to be used here is 'own up', which means to confess a mistake, option B is the right answer. Option A is eliminated, as the sentence needs improvement. Options C and D are eliminated as they do not lend the intended meaning to the given sentence.

questions.question: In the question below, a sentence is given with one part bracketed. Select the option that provides the correct replacement for the bracketed part. In case of no improvement needed, choose Option D. This little prince too had a (narrowly escape) of being stifled by the somewhat rough caresses of its overjoyed young father.
questions.questionHtml:
In the question below, a sentence is given with one part bracketed. Select the option that provides the correct replacement for the bracketed part. In case of no improvement needed, choose Option D.

This little prince too had a (narrowly escape) of being stifled by the somewhat rough caresses of its overjoyed young father.
questions.solution: The noun 'escape' should be used here, instead of the verb 'escaping' or 'escaped'. To modify this noun, the adjective 'narrow' should be used, and not the adverb 'narrowly'. B is the right answer.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement required' as your answer. More times than not, discussions about life tends to be accompanied by the word "balance."
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No improvement required' as your answer.

More times than not, discussions about life tends to be accompanied by the word "balance."
questions.solution: The given phrase is incorrect because 'discussions' is a plural subject and it must be followed by a plural verb, but 'tends' is a singular verb. Similarly, option c) is also incorrect because 'is' is a singular verb. Option a) does not fit in the sentence grammatically owing to the use of present participle form of verb 'tending'. Option b) is grammatically and meaningfully correct. Hence, b) is the correct answer.

questions.questionHtml:

He could never (get by) his brother's death.
questions.solution: Get by - to sustain oneself. Get over - to recover from illness or disappointment or pain. Get out - to leave a place. Get at - imply. Only A makes sense in the context.

questions.solution: Turn out - result. Turn up - appear or arrive. Turn over - to change sides. Turn back - to go in the opposite direction. Only A makes sense in the context.

questions.question: Select the alternative that will improve the underlined part of the sentence. In case there is no improvement required. Select "No improvement". In her essay, MacKinnon wrote that most hurtful for women to organize as women.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the alternative that will improve the underlined part of the sentence. In case there is no improvement required. Select "No improvement".

In her essay, MacKinnon wrote that most hurtful for women to organize as women.
questions.solution: The underlined phrase is incorrect as the phrase needs to have a helping verb to connect it to the remaining part of the sentence. In the phrase in option b) use of the word 'hardening'(means 'make or become hard or harder') is incorrect. In option c) use of the adverb 'substantially' for the noun 'women' is incorrect; instead, an adjective should have been used to make the sentence correct. The phrase in option a) fits both contextually and grammatically in the sentence. Hence, the answer is option a).

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select No improvement. A great deal of what psychologists as researchers and practitioners do in the field is to pay attention s, watch and listen carefully.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select No improvement.

A great deal of what psychologists as researchers and practitioners do in the field is to pay attentions, watch and listen carefully.
questions.solution: The highlighted part is incorrect as use of 'attentions' needs to be replaced by 'attention' as it is an abstract noun (which is always singular). In option b) use of 'paid' is incorrect as infinitive marker 'to' will take a root verb after it. In option d) use of helping verb 'are' is incorrect as helping verb 'are' here is referring to 'what the researchers and practitioners do' in the field, so it will take a singular helping verb i.e. 'is'. Hence, the answer is option c).

questions.question: A part of the sentence is bracketed. Below are given alternatives to the bracketed part which may improve the sentence. Choose the correct alternative. In case no improvement is required, choose " No Improvement " option. She is living (independent from) her parents now.
questions.questionHtml:
A part of the sentence is bracketed. Below are given alternatives to the bracketed part which may improve the sentence. Choose the correct alternative. In case no improvement is required, choose "No Improvement" option.

She is living (independent from) her parents now.
questions.solution:
'Independent' should be followed by 'of' not 'from'. The phrase means to be self-sufficient or separate. The difference between 'Independent from' and 'independent of' is as follows:

Independent from = [not ruled by another country]

The rebel republic has already declared itself independent from the Soviet Union

Independent of = [unaffected by]

Personal conversations are not independent of media news.

Their decisions are quite independent of any other argument.

Therefore, option B is the answer.

questions.solution: The determiner 'all' requires a plural verb after it. So, 'files' would be appropriate in place of 'file'. Hence, option (b) is the answer.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. The government should seek ways to curb spending by candidates and parties, which has reached alarming high levels and poses a threat to free and fair elections.
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

The government should seek ways to curb spending by candidates and parties, which has reached alarming high levels and poses a threat to free and fair elections.
questions.solution: The highlighted part is incorrect as the adjective 'alarming' cannot qualify the other adjective 'high'; the adverb 'alarmingly' is needed here. A is incorrect as the past participle form of verb needs to be used after 'has'. C is incorrect as the noun 'spending' is in singular and we need an auxiliary verb in singular form to agree with it. So, 'has' in place of 'have'. Option B is the right answer.

We decided to call off Tanu yesterday, but it seems she was out.
questions.solution: Call off - cancel or postpone a plan. Call at - grammatically incorrect. Call after - to name a child after someone. Call on - to visit someone. Only C makes sense in the sentence.

questions.question: Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'. She walked quickly to the handwork cupboard and flung off the door .
questions.questionHtml:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement required'.

She walked quickly to the handwork cupboard and flung off the door.
questions.solution: Option A is the right answer. Option D is eliminated, as the sentence needs improvement as 'flung off' is meaningless. Option B is eliminated, as the prepositional phrase 'flung out' would mean to throw something out, which makes no sense in this context. Option C is eliminated since it omits the use of a preposition; 'flung' when used without a preposition, means to throw. It seems absurd if we say that 'she threw the door'.
